Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 49, verse 1:

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O you who have believed, do not put yourselves before Allah and His Messenger.﴾

Tafsir of Surat al-Hujurat

It is a Medinan surah by the consensus of the reciters (qurra'). Thawban narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "I was given the seven long (surahs) in place of the Torah, I was given the mi'un (surahs of about a hundred verses) in place of the Gospel, I was given the mathani (oft-repeated surahs) in place of the Psalms, and my Lord favoured me with the mufassal (the short surahs)."

Some said: the mufassal begins from Surat Muhammad. Most scholars hold that the mufassal begins with this surah. And Allah knows best.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, do not put yourselves before Allah and His Messenger.﴾ Ali ibn Abi Talhah al-Walibi narrated from Ibn Abbas that the meaning of His saying ﴿do not put yourselves before Allah and His Messenger﴾ is: do not say anything contrary to the Book and the Sunnah. Mujahid said: do not presume to decide against Allah and His Messenger until Allah decrees through the tongue of His Messenger what He wills. He said: the meaning of "la tafta'uu" (do not presume) is: do not oppose. It is also said that its meaning is: do not be hasty with speech before the speech of the Messenger, nor with action before the action of the Messenger, and this concerns what is found from him regarding matters of religion, whether in deed or word.

From Qatadah, he said: some people used to say, "If only such-and-such had been revealed, if only such-and-such had been revealed," so Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse. From al-Hasan al-Basri, he said: people slaughtered their sacrifices before the Prophet's prayer on the day of the Eid, so Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse.

From Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that some people fasted on the day of doubt (yawm al-shakk), so Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse.

Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: do not perform the acts of worship before their appointed time. This applies to all acts of worship, except what is supported by evidence from the Sunnah permitting it.

Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr narrated that "a delegation of the Banu Tamim came to the Prophet. Abu Bakr said: O Messenger of Allah, appoint al-Aqra' ibn Habis over them. Umar said: O Messenger of Allah, appoint someone other than the one Abu Bakr mentioned. It is said that the man to whom Umar pointed was al-Qa'qa' ibn Ma'bad ibn Zurarah. Abu Bakr said to Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, 'You only intended to oppose me,' and Umar said, 'I only intended to oppose you,' so they disputed in the presence of the Prophet, and Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse."

Al-Dahhak recited "la tuqaddimu" (with the letters of the verb in the form that reads "do not put forward"), and this is the reading of Ya'qub al-Hadrami; its meaning is: do not advance (la tataqaddamu).

His saying: ﴿And fear Allah; indeed Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾ That is: Hearing of your words, Knowing of what you are upon.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on surah 49, verse 2:

The words of God, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet﴾. In the exegesis: the ignorant Bedouin (al-a'rab) used to come forward before the Prophet and raise their voices ﴿above the voice of the Prophet, and do not speak loudly to him as you speak loudly to one another﴾ above his voice, and they would call him by his name, saying: "O Muhammad! O Abu al-Qasim!" This was a kind of disregard for his right, so God Exalted sent down this verse, that they should address him with the speech of one who honours and exalts him, which indicates the fulfilment of his right in address.

It is narrated that Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas had a hearing impairment and was loud-voiced. When God Exalted sent down this verse, he sat in his house in grief. It is said that he barred his door with iron and said: "I fear that my deeds have been nullified." So the Prophet summoned him and said: "Are you not content to live praiseworthy and die a martyr?" He said: "Yes." He said: "So it shall be." And he was martyred on the Day of al-Yamama.

It is also narrated that he (the Prophet) said to him: "You are of the people of Paradise."

And from Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, that when this verse was revealed he said: "By God, I will not speak to the Messenger of God except as a brother speaks in confidence (ka-akhi al-sirar)."

And from Umar, may God be pleased with him, that after the revelation of this verse he would not speak to the Messenger of God except in a lowered voice, so much so that the Messenger of God would have to ask him to repeat what he was saying.

As for His words: ﴿and do not speak loudly to him as you speak loudly to one another﴾, this is a prohibition against raising the voice in his presence. Some of them said: it is calling him by his name, that is, saying: "O Muhammad! O Abu al-Qasim!" God Exalted forbade that, and commanded that he be called by the title of Prophethood and Messengership. It is related from Malik ibn Anas that he said: whoever says that the Messenger of God was "dirty" (wasikh), intending thereby a deficiency, has disbelieved in God Exalted.

As for His words: ﴿lest your deeds be nullified﴾, meaning: "so that your deeds would be nullified." Thus Ibn Mas'ud also recited it. It is also said: "lest your deeds be nullified."

As for His words: ﴿while you do not perceive﴾, meaning: you do not know that the deeds are being nullified.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 49, verse 3:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who lower their voices in the presence of the Messenger of Allah﴾, meaning: they lower them.

And His saying: ﴿Those are the ones whose hearts Allah has tested for piety﴾, meaning: Allah has purified their hearts for piety. It is also said: Allah tested their hearts and found them sincere. It is also said: what is meant by "hearts" is the possessors of hearts, meaning that Allah, Exalted is He, tested and afflicted them so that they would become pious. The lam here is the lam of outcome (lam al-sayrurah), and this is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So that it would become for them an enemy and a source of grief﴾.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For them is forgiveness and a great reward﴾, its meaning is clear.

The Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 49, verse 4:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who call out to you from behind the private chambers﴾. The exegetes mention that the delegation of Tamim came to the Prophet and began calling out to him from behind the private chambers, "O Muhammad, O Muhammad, come out to us." Among them were Qays ibn 'Asim al-Minqari, al-Zibriqan ibn Badr, al-Aqra' ibn Habis, al-Qa'qa' ibn Ma'bad, and others.

It is related that al-Aqra' ibn Habis said: "O Muhammad, my praise is an adornment and my blame is a disgrace." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "That is Allah."

And His saying: ﴿Most of them do not use their reason﴾. That is, they are a people most of whom do not use their reason. It is said: among them were those who, when they knew, understood and comprehended, and among them were those who neither reasoned nor knew even when they knew. Therefore He said: ﴿most of them do not use their reason﴾, even though they knew and reasoned.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 49, verse 5:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Had they been patient until you came out to them, it would have been better for them﴾. It is related that the Prophet dispatched a detachment (sariyya), and they seized captives from (Bal'amar) ibn Ghanm. Their men came seeking ransom and began calling out: "O Muhammad, O Muhammad, come out to us, we will ransom you." So he came out, released some of the captives and ransomed others. He had intended to release all of them, but when they behaved discourteously, he released some of them and ransomed others. This is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Had they been patient until you came out to them, it would have been better for them﴾, that is: it would have been better for them, in that he would have released all of the captives.

As for His saying: ﴿And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾, its meaning is apparent. In these verses is a clarification of the use of good manners (adab) in the presence of the Prophet. Some have mentioned the gravity of the offence in neglecting that, and what leads to the nullification of deeds and the deserving of punishment. The Companions of the Messenger of Allah used to be reverent and would hesitate to speak in his presence, and they would love for a Bedouin from the desert to come and ask the Messenger of Allah about something so that they could hear the answer, because they were reluctant to ask.

In the hadith of Dhu al-Yadayn, that he said to the Messenger of Allah when he concluded the prayer after two rak'ahs: "Has the prayer been shortened, or have you forgotten?" Abu Bakr and Umar were among the people, and the notables of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, and they hesitated to speak to him, but this man spoke, because he did not know of his station and the greatness of his right as they knew it.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 49, verse 6:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, if a grave sinner (fasiq) comes to you with information, verify it﴾. The people of tafsir said: The verse was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt. The Messenger of Allah sent him to the Banu al-Mustaliq of Khuza'ah to collect their zakat (alms), and there was a grudge (ihnah) between him and them in the Jahiliyyah. When he drew near to them, and they heard of his approach, they came out to meet him to honour him. He feared them and returned, and he said to the Messenger: "O Messenger of Allah, they have withheld the zakat." In another narration: "They have apostatised from Islam and have not given anything." So the Prophet (ﷺ) sent a detachment (sariyyah) under Khalid ibn al-Walid to them, and commanded him to ascertain their condition. If they were as al-Walid had said, he was to fight them. Khalid went and came to them by night, and he heard the voice of the callers to prayer among them, and he heard the recitation of the Qur'an. So he returned and informed the Prophet, and Allah, may He be exalted, revealed this verse. It has also been narrated that when the Prophet heard the statement of al-Walid, he became angry and sent someone to fight them, so Allah, may He be exalted, revealed this verse. Qatadah and others mentioned this. It is related from the Messenger of Allah that he said after this: "Deliberation is from Allah, and haste is from Shaytan."

As for His saying: ﴿if a grave sinner comes to you﴾, they said: the fasiq here is the liar (al-kadhdhab). As for the linguistic meaning, we have already explained that it is one who departs from the obedience of Allah.

As for His saying: ﴿verify (fatabayyanu)﴾, it has been recited as "fatathabbatu" (be steadfast/confirm), and the two meanings are close. It means abandoning haste, and reflecting and taking one's time in the matter.

As for His saying: ﴿lest you harm a people in ignorance﴾, its meaning is: lest you afflict a people in ignorance. The meaning of "harm" (isabah) here is harm to life and property through killing, capture and plunder.

As for His saying: ﴿and then become regretful for what you have done﴾, i.e., you become regretful for your action. What is intended is not the morning (isbah) which is the opposite of evening.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 49, verses 7–8:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And know that among you is the Messenger of Allah. If he were to obey you in much of the affair, you would be in distress﴾, meaning: you would be destroyed. It was also said: you would go astray and be misguided. It is said: hardship and difficulty would befall you.

His saying ﴿obey you﴾ is a kind of metaphor (majaz), because obedience in its reality is the act of the lesser in agreeing with the word of the greater. It is related from some of the early generations (salaf) that he said: "How excellent a Lord is our Lord; if we obeyed Him, He would not disobey us." This is in the manner of metaphor and expansion in speech. The poet said:

(Many a one whose chest has become full of rage, / Even if he wished for my death, he would not be obeyed.)

Meaning: he would not attain what he wished for. This is in the manner of metaphor.

His saying ﴿But Allah has made the faith beloved to you﴾: it is said that He made it beloved by establishing the proofs of His oneness and guiding them to it. It is also said: He made it beloved by mentioning the reward and the true promise.

His saying ﴿and has made it fair-seeming in your hearts﴾, so that they accepted it and preferred it over other things. The nature of the human being is disposed to choose what is made attractive in his heart. When Allah guided the believers to faith and inclined their hearts toward it, until they accepted it, He called that making faith attractive in their hearts.

His saying ﴿and has made disbelief hateful to you﴾: it is said that He made disbelief hateful by mentioning the threat and warning against committing it.

His saying ﴿and wickedness and disobedience﴾: wickedness (fusuq) is everything by which a person becomes a transgressor, i.e., goes out of obedience to Allah. Disobedience (ισyan, ʿiṣyān) is opposing the command.

His saying ﴿Those are the rightly guided, by bounty from Allah and favor﴾, meaning: those are the rightly guided, by His grace and bestowal.

His saying ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise﴾, meaning: All-Knowing of His creation, All-Wise in what He arranges for them.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 49, verse 9:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight, then make peace between them﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others said: the verse was revealed concerning the Aws and the Khazraj, who had a fight between them with palm stalks, sandals and fists over a matter they disputed among themselves.

﴿of the believers fight, then make peace between them﴾

Another, namely Qatadah, said: it was revealed concerning two men who quarrelled during the time of the Prophet over a right between them. One of them said to the other: "I will certainly take it from you by force, relying on the multitude of my kin." The other said: "No, rather I will bring you to judgement before the Messenger of Allah." The matter between them kept escalating until they leapt upon each other and struck each other, and there was fighting between them with sandals and hands. Then Allah the Exalted revealed this verse.

Mujahid said: the ṭā'ifah (group) is a term applying to one person up to a thousand or more.

It is narrated that when the Prophet arrived in Madinah, it was said to him: "If only you would go to ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul and call him to faith." So he mounted a donkey and set out towards him, and the land was salty, and his companions were around him, so the dust rose. When he reached the place where ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul was, with a group around him, he said: "Keep away from us, O Muhammad! The stench of your donkey has harmed us." ʿAbd Allah ibn Rawahah said: "By Allah, his donkey is more fragrant (in scent) than you!" A group grew angry for ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, and a group for ʿAbd Allah ibn Rawahah, and evil erupted between them, and they fought with staves, sandals and the like. The Prophet wished to calm them but was unable to, then they calmed down, and Allah the Exalted revealed this verse. Al-Bukhari mentioned in the Sahih a report, related through Anas, close to this concerning the occasion of the revelation of this verse. Allah the Exalted called that fighting (muqatalah) because pursuing it leads to killing. What we have mentioned about the story of ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul and ʿAbd Allah ibn Rawahah was related by al-Kalbi, Muqatil and others.

His words: ﴿then make peace between them﴾, meaning: strive to repel the corruption and remove the evil. Know that when such a thing occurs between two groups, it is obligatory upon the imam, or one who deputises for the imam, to examine between them and bring them to the truth. If one of the two groups refuses to accept the truth, he returns it to the truth first by speech, then he ascends step by step until it reaches fighting. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿But if one of them transgresses against the other, then fight the one that transgresses until it returns to the command of Allah﴾, meaning: returns to the command of Allah.

His words: ﴿And if it returns﴾, meaning: it turns back, and its meaning: it submits to the truth.

His words: ﴿then make peace between them with justice﴾, meaning: with truth.

His words: ﴿and act justly﴾, meaning: and be equitable.

His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly﴾, meaning: those who are equitable. And in a report from the Prophet, he said: "Those who act justly will be on pulpits of light on the right hand of the Most Merciful on the Day of Resurrection. It was said: 'Who are they, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'Those who were just in their judgement, regarding themselves, their families and whatever they were put in charge of.'"

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 49, verse 10:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The believers are but brothers﴾, meaning: in allegiance, mutual support and mercy. This is in the sense of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The believing men and the believing women are allies of one another﴾. It is also reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The believer to the believer is like a building, one part of it strengthening another." And it is reported from him, peace and blessings be upon him, that he said: "The believers are like one soul: when one part of it complains, the rest of it responds to it with wakefulness and fever."

It is established, through the transmission of Ibn 'Umar, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The Muslim is the brother of the Muslim. He does not wrong him, nor does he humiliate him. Whoever is in the need of his Muslim brother, Allah is in his need. Whoever relieves a Muslim of a difficulty, Allah will relieve him of a distress on the Day of Resurrection. And whoever conceals [the fault of] a Muslim, Allah will conceal him on the Day of Resurrection." Related by al-Bukhari and Muslim.

His saying: ﴿So make peace between your two brothers﴾. Mentioning the two brothers indicates, by the obligation of reconciliation between them, the obligation of reconciliation among a large group.

His saying: ﴿And fear Allah﴾, meaning: fear Allah lest you leave them in corruption, and strive in seeking reform.

His saying: ﴿That you may receive mercy﴾, meaning: that Allah, Exalted is He, may turn His kindness toward you and pardon you. It is also said that ﴿make peace between your two brothers﴾ means "your brethren." Asbat related from al-Suddi that a man from the Ansar had a wife who wished to visit her family, but her husband prevented her and confined her in an upper room. Her family came to take her to them, and the man sought help from his people in preventing her; so strife and fighting broke out between them, and Allah, Exalted is He, revealed this verse.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 49, verse 11:

The words of the Most High: ﴿O you who have believed, let not a people ridicule [another] people﴾. Al-sukhriyya is al-istihza' (mockery), and al-batar, meaning al-muhana (humiliation) and al-ihtiqar (contempt).

And His words: ﴿a people [ridicule] a people﴾. Al-qawm (people) here means men, as the poet said:

(I do not know, and I do not think I know, / Are they the people of Hisn or women?)

Men were called qawm rather than women because they are the ones who stand up (yaqumuna) to affairs.

Mujahid said: the verse concerns mockery, the rich mocking the poor and the strong mocking the weak.

It is also said: it is the mockery of the cunning (al-dahat) toward the people of simple hearts.

﴿...a people [ridicule] a people, who may be better than them; nor let women [ridicule] women, who may be better than them. And do not defame one another, nor insult one another by nicknames﴾.

And His words: ﴿who may be better than them﴾ mean: perhaps the one being mocked is better than the one mocking.

And His words: ﴿nor let women [ridicule] women﴾ mean: nor let women mock women, perhaps she who is mocked is better than her who mocks; that is, perhaps the one mocked is better than the mocker. The intended meaning is in the Hereafter.

It is reported in a khabar that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Abu Dharr: "Look at the lowliest man in the mosque beside you." He pointed to a poor man wearing shabby clothes. He said: "Look at the most exalted man in the mosque beside you." He pointed to one of the wealthy, dressed in finery. He said: "This one is better on the Day of Resurrection than a whole earth full of the like of that one." And by this he meant the poor man.

And His words: ﴿nor defame one another﴾ mean: (do not disparage) one another, like His words: ﴿nor kill yourselves﴾, meaning: do not kill one another.

Al-Dahhak said: do not curse one another. It is also said: do not slander one another.

And His words: ﴿nor insult one another by nicknames﴾. Al-nabz and al-laqab have the same meaning.

The meaning of nabz here is the disliked nickname which a person dislikes being called by. And concerning ﴿Wretched is the name of disobedience after faith﴾: Abu Jubayra al-Ansari said: "The Messenger of Allah came to us in Madina, and each of us had one name, two names, or three names, and the Messenger of Allah would call him by that name. It was said to him: 'He becomes angry when he is called by this.' So he left that, and Allah the Most High revealed this verse."

Mujahid and al-Hasan said: it is that one says to a man who has become Muslim: "O Jew! O Christian!", reproaching him with what he was upon before. Qatada and Abu al-'Aliya said: it is that one says: "O hypocrite! O sinner!" In some tafsirs: there was a dispute between Ka'b ibn Malik and Abd Allah ibn Abi Hadrad al-Aslami. Ka'b ibn Malik said to Abd Allah: "O bedouin!" and Abd Allah said to Ka'b: "O Jew!" So Allah the Most High revealed this verse and forbade them from such things. In some reports it is related from the Prophet that he said: "Among the rights of a Muslim over a Muslim is that he calls him by his most beloved names."

And His words: ﴿Wretched is the name of disobedience after faith﴾. Whoever says that the sinner (al-fasiq) cannot be a believer has used this as evidence, saying: "If the sinner were a believer, the words ﴿after faith﴾ would not be proper." The answer: what is meant is the prohibition of saying "O sinner! O hypocrite!" As if He said: wretched is the description of sinfulness after belief in Allah. Some said: "ba'd" (after) here means "ma'a" (with), and its meaning is: wretched is the name of disobedience together with faith.

And His words: ﴿And whoever does not repent, then those are the wrongdoers﴾, meaning: whoever does not repent of these things which they used to do in the Jahiliyya, then those are the wrongdoers.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 49, verse 12:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, avoid much of [what may be] suspicion; indeed, some suspicion is sin﴾. It is established by the narration of Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet said: "Beware of suspicion, for suspicion is the most false of speech."

And in some reports: "If you feel envy, do not act upon it; if you look at a [forbidden] thing, pass on; and if you suspect, do not verify it."

And from Anas that the Prophet said: "Guard yourselves against people through bad opinion." This is a gharib (unusual) report.

And from Salman al-Farisi, who said: "Indeed, I count the pieces of meat in the pot out of fear of bad suspicion." And from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "Silence is better than suspicion." And from Abu al-'Aliyah al-Riyahi, that he would seal [his mouth] for seven breaths so that he would not harbour an evil suspicion.

﴿...some suspicion is sin, and do not spy﴾

Know that the suspicion forbidden is evil suspicion toward people of goodness; as for people of evil, it is permissible.

His saying: ﴿indeed, some suspicion is sin﴾ means: this suspicion.

His saying: ﴿and do not spy﴾. Tajassus (spying) is searching out the faults (awrat) of people, as stated by Mujahid. Ibn Sirin recited: "wa la tahassasu" with the letter ha'. They differed concerning tajassus and tahassus. Some said: they are one and the same. Others distinguished, saying: tajassus is searching out the faults of people, as we have mentioned, while tahassus is listening to the conversation of a people. It is also said: tajassus is searching out matters, while tahassus is perceiving by one of the senses. And it is established from the Prophet, by the narration of Anas, that he said: "Do not sever ties, do not turn your backs on one another, do not hate one another, do not envy one another, do not spy on one another, and be, O servants of Allah, brothers." The Shaykh, the Imam, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Al-Shaykh Abu 'Ali al-Shafi'i informed us in Mecca, Abu al-Hasan ibn Faras informed us, Abu Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad 'Abd Allah ibn Yazid al-Muqri' informed us, from his grandfather, from Muhammad, from Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah, from al-Zuhri, from Anas... the hadith.

In some reports: 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, went out at night on patrol (ya'assu) accompanied by 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf. They passed by a house from which we heard noise and voices. 'Umar said: "I think they are drinking wine. What shall we do?" 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf said: "I think we have committed what we were forbidden from, namely spying," and they returned.

In this report, that house was the house of Rabi'ah ibn Umayyah ibn Khalaf.

In another report it was said to Ibn Mas'ud: "Would you like [to see] al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah, whose beard is dripping with wine?" Al-Walid was the governor of Kufa, and Ibn Mas'ud was its jurist. He said: "We have been forbidden from spying."

﴿And do not backbite one another﴾

His saying: ﴿and do not backbite one another﴾. Ghibah (backbiting) is that one mentions his brother in his absence with what he would dislike if he heard it. In the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, the Prophet was asked about backbiting, and he said: "Your mentioning your brother with what he dislikes." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, what if what I say is true of my brother?" He said: "If what you say is in your brother, then you have backbitten him; and if what you say is not in your brother, then you have slandered him."

In the reports: a woman entered upon 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, and when she left, 'A'ishah said: "How lovely she is, were it not for her shortness." The Prophet said: "You have backbitten her, so seek forgiveness from Allah." And it is narrated from the Prophet that he said: "If one of you backbites his brother, let him ask forgiveness for him, for that is its expiation."

And in some reports also from the Prophet that he said: "Beware of backbiting, for backbiting is worse than fornication; the fornicator commits fornication, then repents, and Allah accepts his repentance; but the one who backbites will not be forgiven until the one he backbit forgives him." That is, pardons him.

And it has come in reports: "There is no backbiting of a sinner."

And he said: "Mention the wicked person with what is in him, so that people may beware of him."

The scholars said: there is no backbiting of three: the oppressive ruler, the openly sinful person, and the one who introduces an innovation (bid'ah) into Islam.

Likewise the scholars said: if a person asks another for a valid purpose, there is no harm in mentioning what is in him. Ghibah is derived from ghayb (absence); as if, when one mentions a person in his absence with what would displease him, that mention is backbiting. The early generation (al-salaf) were extremely cautious about such matters. It is related that two physicians entered upon Ibn Sirin, and when they left he said: "Were it not that it would be backbiting, I would have mentioned which of them is the better physician." And from Mu'awiyah ibn Qurrah, who said: "If a one-armed man entered upon you and you said after he had left, 'This one-armed man,' you would have backbitten him." Abu Ishaq said: "He is right," meaning al-Sabi'i. The scholars said: if one says "So-and-so al-A'mash" or "So-and-so al-A'war" or "So-and-so al-Butayn," intending by that to identify him, and he cannot be identified except by it, there is no harm. And some imams of hadith, when narrating from Muslim al-Butayn, would say: "Muslim narrated to us," and gesture with his hands to indicate the bulkiness of the belly.

And Ibn Sirin mentioned Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and placed his hand over his eye, for Ibrahim was one-eyed, and said: "I saw him in that very state, and no one after him was like him."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Would any of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother? You would detest it﴾. That is: just as one of you dislikes eating the flesh of his brother while he is dead, so let him likewise dislike mentioning him with evil while he is absent. If someone asks: what is the similarity between the two in meaning? The answer: when one eats his flesh while he is dead, he has violated his sanctity, and he is unaware of it; and when he mentions him with evil in his absence, he has violated his sanctity, and he is unaware of it. It is related from 'Amr ibn al-'As that he passed by a dead donkey and said: "For one of you to fill his belly with this flesh is better for him than to backbite his brother." And it is said of the one who backbites in the language: "So-and-so eats the flesh of people." And in the tafsir a verse is cited on this meaning:

(If they eat my flesh, their flesh is torn; and if they demolish my glory, I build for them glory.)

His saying: ﴿And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is Accepting of repentance, Merciful﴾. That is: He accepts repentance from His creation and is kind to them.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 49, verse 13:

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿O mankind, indeed We have created you from male and female﴾, meaning Adam and Eve, peace be upon them both, ﴿and made you peoples and tribes﴾. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The shu'ub (peoples) are the large groupings, like Mudar and Rabi'ah, and the qaba'il (tribes) are the subdivisions among them, like Tamim from Mudar and Shaybān from Rabi'ah." Some said: "The shu'ub are those furthest in lineage, and the qaba'il are those closest in lineage." It is also reported from some of them that the shu'ub are among the non-Arabs ('ajam) and the qaba'il are among the Arabs. The singular of shu'ub is sha'b, and sha'b with a fatha on the shin and with a kasra on it, and it is derived from tasha''ub (branching out).

His statement: ﴿that you may know one another﴾, meaning that some of you may recognize others. Al-A'mash read: "litata'arafū" (lit-ta'ārafū). Ibn 'Abbas read: "lita'rifū" (li-ta'rifū). It was said that, according to this reading: "that you may know that the most honoured of you before God is the most righteous of you" (with a fatha on the alif). The sound reading is the first one, and the meaning of the verse is the cutting off of boasting by ancestry and lineages.

His statement: ﴿Indeed the most honoured of you before God is the most righteous of you﴾. In a report, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "God, may He be exalted, says on the Day of Resurrection: 'The people of the gathering will know who is most worthy of honour; where are the righteous?'"

In another report: God, may He be exalted, says on the Day of Resurrection: "O people, you raised up your lineages and lowered My lineage; so today I will raise My lineage and lower your lineages; where are the righteous?"

In the exegesis (tafsir) it is mentioned: that Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas had deafness, and he loved to draw near to the Messenger of God in order to hear his speech. One day he came when the people had taken their seats, so he began to push between the people to get close to the Messenger of God. A man said to him: "Sit where the gathering has brought you to." He said to him: "Who are you?" The man said: "I am so-and-so." He said: "The son of so-and-so," and he mentioned a mother of his from the Jahiliyyah whom he used to be reproached for. The Messenger of God heard that, and said: "O Thabit, look at the people." So he looked, and the Prophet said: "You have no superiority over them except through piety (taqwa)."

This has been mentioned as the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of His statement: ﴿and do not defame one another﴾. Taqwa (piety) is abstaining from everything that God has forbidden. The people of knowledge have said: lineage may confer superiority in this world, in the sense that a person of non-noble descent is not a suitable match (kufu') for one of noble descent; and when noble and non-noble candidates are together for leadership (imamah), the one of noble descent is preferred if they are equal in knowledge and piety. As for the Hereafter, there is no superiority for noble descent; superiority belongs only to piety.

His statement: ﴿Indeed God is All-Knowing, All-Aware﴾, its meaning is evident.

The Exalted's statement: ﴿The Bedouins say, "We have believed." Say, "You have not believed; rather say, 'We have submitted (aslamna),'"﴾ That is: "We have surrendered (istaslamna) and obeyed (qadana)." The verse was revealed concerning a people who would display faith with their tongues while not affirming it in their hearts.

The scholars differed regarding faith (iman) and Islam (islam). Some of them said: they are one and the same, while others distinguished between them. In some reports from the Prophet (ﷺ) he said: "Islam is outward, and faith is in the heart." And it is related from al-Zuhri: Islam is the utterance of the word, and faith is the action. And in the report of Jibril (peace be upon him), when he came asking about Islam and faith, the Messenger (ﷺ) distinguished between them, making Islam the outward acts and faith the inward affirmation. This is a sound report.

It is also established that the Prophet (ﷺ) gave to a group of people and did not give to a man. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas said: "You gave to so-and-so and so-and-so, and you did not give to so-and-so, and he is a believer?" He said: "Or a Muslim." Those who said they are one and the same used as evidence the Exalted's statement: ﴿So We brought out those who were in it of the believers. And We found not in it except one house of Muslims.﴾ Most of the reports indicate a distinction, so it is permissible to distinguish them as we have said, in accordance with what has come in the reports. And it is permissible to say they are one and the same, so that Islam carries the meaning of faith and faith carries the meaning of Islam, and this is the common understanding among Muslims, that one of them is understood as the other is understood. And Allah knows best.

As for His statement: ﴿And faith has not yet entered your hearts﴾, it is evidence that they were not affirming in their inward being.

As for His statement: ﴿And if you obey Allah and His Messenger, He will not deprive you (yalitkum) of anything of your deeds.﴾ It was also read as "la yalitkum," meaning: He will not diminish you.

As for the one who read "la ya'latkum min a'malikum shay'an," it also carries the meaning of diminishing. The poet said:

(And a night of travel, you traveled through it, and the Layth did not deprive you of its journey)

His statement: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ is clear in meaning.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 49, verse 15:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the believers are only those who have believed in Allah and His Messenger and then have not doubted⦆ — meaning: they affirmed and did not waver.

And His saying: ﴿and strive with their wealth and their lives in the cause of Allah⦆ — meaning: they sacrificed their selves and expended their wealth in seeking the pleasure of Allah.

And His saying: ﴿It is those who are the truthful⦆ — meaning: they are the ones who are verified (muhaqqiqun) in faith. It is as though, when He mentioned the hypocrites in the first verse, He then mentioned the attribute of the verified believers in this verse, [so as to express] the desire for Him.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 49, verse 16:

The Almighty's saying: ﴿Say: Will you inform Allah of your religion?﴾ Here "ʿalima" (knew) is used in the sense of "aʿlama" (inform).

And His saying: ﴿And Allah knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and Allah is All-Knowing of everything.﴾ That is, ʿAlim (All-Knowing). They used to say: "Islam is such-and-such, and we have submitted," and "Faith is such-and-such, and we have believed." So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse.

The Qur'an says: ﴿They consider it a favour to you that they have embraced Islam.﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 49, verse 17:

The words of the Most High: ﴿They consider it a favour to you that they have embraced Islam.﴾ Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others said: The verse was revealed concerning some Bedouins of the tribe of Banu Asad who used to say: "O Messenger of Allah, we have believed in you, and we have not fought against you as Banu so-and-so and Banu so-and-so fought against you." So Allah the Most High revealed this verse, and they used to say that as a favour upon him (ﷺ).

In another narration: Some Bedouins came to Madina in a large group, and they raised the prices and blocked the roads. They used to say: "O Messenger of Allah, we have believed in you, so give us such-and-such." So Allah the Most High revealed this verse.

His words: ﴿Say: Do not consider your Islam a favour to me. Rather, Allah has bestowed a favour upon you that He has guided you to faith.﴾ That is: It is He who has blessed you by bringing you out of disbelief into faith.

His words: ﴿If you are truthful.﴾ Its meaning: Know that the favour belongs to Allah over you, if you are truthful that you have believed in Allah.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 49, verse 18:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah knows the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾. This has been mentioned before. 

Abdullah ibn Dinar narrated from Ibn Umar that the Prophet (ﷺ) gave a sermon on the day of the Conquest of Makkah and said: "O people, indeed Allah has removed from you the arrogance of the Jahiliyyah (the Age of Ignorance) and its boasting in ancestors. So people are of two kinds: a righteous, God-fearing person who is noble before Allah, and a wicked, miserable person who is contemptible before Allah. And people are the children of Adam, and Adam was created from dust." Then he recited the words of the Exalted: ﴿O people, indeed We have created you from a male and a female﴾, [up to the end of] the verse.

Samurah ibn Jundub narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Lineage (al-hasab): wealth; and nobility (al-karam): piety."

Abu Isa al-Tirmidhi reported these two reports in his Jami' in the tafsir of this surah.
